content: The identification and characterization of the causative agents responsible for infections are critical for the early detection of outbreaks. This process is particularly important when identifying the specific pathogen involved and/or distinct patterns of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Such efforts also provide valuable data on the local epidemiology of healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and AMR patterns, which can inform the development of relevant policies and action plans. Data on antimicrobial consumption can be utilized to create antibiotic formulary guidelines and action plans aimed at combating AMR. National infection prevention and control (IPC) programs should be active, independent, and clearly defined, with specific objectives, functions, and activities. These programs are essential for preventing HAIs and addressing AMR through the implementation of good IPC practices. Furthermore, national IPC programs should be integrated with other relevant national programs and professional organizations. Although there is limited evidence evaluating the effectiveness of comprehensive national IPC programs, experts and country representatives have provided clear examples where sustained national IPC programs have successfully reduced HAI rates and infections caused by multidrug-resistant organisms. Therefore, it is strongly recommended that every country establish a standalone, active national IPC program to prevent HAIs, combat AMR, and ensure safe, high-quality healthcare delivery. The organization of national IPC programs must include clear objectives, designated infection preventionists, and a defined scope of responsibilities. Minimum objectives should include goals for reducing endemic and epidemic infections and the development of evidence-based recommendations for IPC processes and practices known to prevent HAIs and limit the spread of AMR. The technical team responsible for the IPC program should consist of trained infection preventionists, including medical and nursing professionals, with formal IPC training and allocated time for their tasks. This team should have decision-making authority, a dedicated budget, and support from national authorities and leaders. The International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005) and the WHO Global Action Plan on AMR (2015) emphasize the importance of IPC as a central component of health system capacity building and preparedness. This includes developing national plans for HAI prevention, strengthening national IPC policies and standards, and monitoring adherence to these policies. National IPC activities are essential for preventing HAIs and AMR among patients, healthcare workers, and visitors. The IHR requires member states to notify the WHO of events that may constitute a public health emergency of international concern and highlights the importance of IPC practices in healthcare facilities for containment. The current IHR monitoring and assessment tool includes IPC as a key indicator, and IPC is expected to feature prominently in future approaches. Linkages between national IPC programs and other related programs are crucial and should include areas such as water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH), environmental authorities, AMR containment (including antimicrobial stewardship programs), tuberculosis, HIV, and other priority public health programs. Collaboration with scientific professional organizations, training establishments, and relevant sub-national bodies is also essential. The development and dissemination of technical evidence-based guidelines for IPC should be informed by local risk assessments and adapted to local conditions. These guidelines should include standard precautions such as hand hygiene, use of personal protective equipment, sterilization, safe handling of linen, healthcare waste management, respiratory hygiene, environmental cleaning, and prevention of injuries from sharp instruments. Transmission-based precautions and aseptic techniques for clinical procedures should also be included. National IPC programs must support advanced educational programs on IPC. Training should target three categories of human resources: IPC specialists, all healthcare workers involved in patient care, and administrative and managerial staff responsible for healthcare safety and quality. Early stakeholder participation in the development of national standards and guidelines can facilitate consensus and implementation. The national IPC team should lead key activities, including HAI and AMR surveillance, implementation of standard and transmission-based precautions, development of national technical guidelines, outbreak prevention and response, healthcare worker training, and monitoring compliance with IPC practices. Adequate procurement of IPC supplies and collaboration with relevant ministries are also necessary. Good quality microbiological support, provided by at least one national reference laboratory, is critical for an effective IPC program. This includes the identification and characterization of pathogens and AMR patterns, which are essential for early outbreak detection and microbiological confirmation. Strict adherence to laboratory standards and biosafety measures is vital for reliable microbiological techniques and unbiased result interpretation. The development and implementation of evidence-based IPC guidelines, supported by healthcare worker education and adherence monitoring, are strongly recommended to reduce HAIs and AMR. Guidelines should be adapted to local conditions for effective uptake and implementation.
